entries.7961e964601908af024a156374da04df3f6fbd4e: <div sID="gen2011" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Exod.29" sID="Exod.29"/> <div eID="gen2011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2012" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2013" type="x-p"/> Particular orders are given in this chapter, I. Concerning the consecration of the priests, and the sanctification of the altar, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.1-Exod.29.37">ver. 1-37</reference>. II. Concerning the daily sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.41">ver. 38-41</reference>. To which gracious promises are annexed that God would own and bless them in all their services, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.42-Exod.29.46">ver. 42</reference>, &c.

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2014" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the thing that thou shalt do unto them to hallow them, to minister unto me in the priest's office: Take one young bullock, and two rams without blemish, 2 And unleavened bread, and cakes unleavened tempered with oil, and wafers unleavened anointed with oil: <hi type="italic">of</hi> wheaten flour shalt thou make them. <hi type="super">3</hi> And thou shalt put them into one basket, and bring them in the basket, with the bullock and the two rams. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Aaron and his sons thou shalt bring unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, and shalt wash them with water. <hi type="super">5</hi> And thou shalt take the garments, and put upon Aaron the coat, and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastplate, and gird him with the curious girdle of the ephod: 6 And thou shalt put the mitre upon his head, and put the holy crown upon the mitre. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then shalt thou take the anointing oil, and pour <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon his head, and anoint him. 8 And thou shalt bring his sons, and put coats upon them. 9 And thou shalt gird them with girdles, Aaron and his sons, and put the bonnets on them: and the priest's office shall be theirs for a perpetual statute: and thou shalt consecrate Aaron and his sons. <hi type="super">10</hi> And thou shalt cause a bullock to be brought before the tabernacle of the congregation: and Aaron and his sons shall put their hands upon the head of the bullock. <hi type="super">11</hi> And thou shalt kill the bullock before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">by</hi> the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">12</hi> And thou shalt take of the blood of the bullock, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the horns of the altar with thy finger, and pour all the blood beside the bottom of the altar. 13 And thou shalt take all the fat that covereth the inwards, and the caul <hi type="italic">that is</hi> above the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat that <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon them, and burn <hi type="italic">them</hi> upon the altar. <hi type="super">14</hi> But the flesh of the bullock, and his skin, and his dung, shalt thou burn with fire without the camp: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a sin offering. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou shalt also take one ram; and Aaron and his sons shall put their hands upon the head of the ram. <hi type="super">16</hi> And thou shalt slay the ram, and thou shalt take his blood, and sprinkle <hi type="italic">it</hi> round about upon the altar. <hi type="super">17</hi> And thou shalt cut the ram in pieces, and wash the inwards of him, and his legs, and put <hi type="italic">them</hi> unto his pieces, and unto his head. <hi type="super">18</hi> And thou shalt burn the whole ram upon the altar: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a burnt offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a sweet savour, an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">19</hi> And thou shalt take the other ram; and Aaron and his sons shall put their hands upon the head of the ram. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then shalt thou kill the ram, and take of his blood, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron, and upon the tip of the right ear of his sons, and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot, and sprinkle the blood upon the altar round about. <hi type="super">21</hi> And thou shalt take of the blood that <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the altar, and of the anointing oil, and sprinkle <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon Aaron, and upon his garments, and upon his sons, and upon the garments of his sons with him: and he shall be hallowed, and his garments, and his sons, and his sons' garments with him. 22 Also thou shalt take of the ram the fat and the rump, and the fat that covereth the inwards, and the caul <hi type="italic">above</hi> the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat that <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon them, and the right shoulder; for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a ram of consecration: 23 And one loaf of bread, and one cake of oiled bread, and one wafer out of the basket of the unleavened bread that <hi type="italic">is</hi> before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">24</hi> And thou shalt put all in the hands of Aaron, and in the hands of his sons; and shalt wave them <hi type="italic">for</hi> a wave offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">25</hi> And thou shalt receive them of their hands, and burn <hi type="italic">them</hi> upon the altar for a burnt offering, for a sweet savour before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it <hi type="italic">is</hi> an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">26</hi> And thou shalt take the breast of the ram of Aaron's consecration, and wave it <hi type="italic">for</hi> a wave offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and it shall be thy part. <hi type="super">27</hi> And thou shalt sanctify the breast of the wave offering, and the shoulder of the heave offering, which is waved, and which is heaved up, of the ram of the consecration, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of <hi type="italic">that</hi> which <hi type="italic">is</hi> for Aaron, and of <hi type="italic">that</hi> which is for his sons: <hi type="super">28</hi> And it shall be Aaron's and his sons' by a statute for ever from the children of Israel: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> an heave offering: and it shall be an heave offering from the children of Israel of the sacrifice of their peace offerings, <hi type="italic">even</hi> their heave offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">29</hi> And the holy garments of Aaron shall be his sons' after him, to be anointed therein, and to be consecrated in them. 30 <hi type="italic">And</hi> that son that is priest in his stead shall put them on seven days, when he cometh into the tabernacle of the congregation to minister in the holy <hi type="italic">place.</hi> <hi type="super">31</hi> And thou shalt take the ram of the consecration, and seethe his flesh in the holy place. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Aaron and his sons shall eat the flesh of the ram, and the bread that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the basket, <hi type="italic">by</hi> the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">33</hi> And they shall eat those things wherewith the atonement was made, to consecrate <hi type="italic">and</hi> to sanctify them: but a stranger shall not eat <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> because they <hi type="italic">are</hi> holy. <hi type="super">34</hi> And if ought of the flesh of the consecrations, or of the bread, remain unto the morning, then thou shalt burn the remainder with fire: it shall not be eaten, because it <hi type="italic">is</hi> holy. <hi type="super">35</hi> And thus shalt thou do unto Aaron, and to his sons, according to all <hi type="italic">things</hi> which I have commanded thee: seven days shalt thou consecrate them. <hi type="super">36</hi> And thou shalt offer every day a bullock <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sin offering for atonement: and thou shalt cleanse the altar, when thou hast made an atonement for it, and thou shalt anoint it, to sanctify it. <hi type="super">37</hi> Seven days thou shalt make an atonement for the altar, and sanctify it; and it shall be an altar most holy: whatsoever toucheth the altar shall be holy. <div eID="gen2014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2015" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The law concerning the consecration of Aaron and his sons to the priest's office, which was to be done with a great deal of ceremony and solemnity, that they themselves might be duly affected with the greatness of the work to which they were called, and that the people also might learn to magnify the office and none might dare to invade it. <div eID="gen2015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2016" type="x-p"/> 1. The ceremonies wherewith it was to be done were very fully and particularly appointed, because nothing of this kind had been done before, and because it was to be a statute for ever that the high priest should be thus inaugurated. Now, <div eID="gen2016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2017" type="x-p"/> (1.) The work to be done was the consecrating of the persons whom God had chosen to be priests, by which they devoted and gave up themselves to the service of God and God declared his acceptance of them; and the people were made to know that they <hi type="italic">glorified not themselves</hi> to be made priests, but were <hi type="italic">called of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.4-Heb.5.5">Heb. v. 4, 5</reference>. They were thus distinguished from common men, sequestered from common services, and set apart for God and an immediate attendance on him. Note, All that are to be employed for God are to be sanctified to him. The person must first be accepted, and then the performance. The Hebrew phrase for consecrating <hi type="italic">is filling the hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt fill the hand of Aaron and his sons,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">ram of consecration</hi> is the <hi type="italic">ram of fillings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.29.22">v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.26">26</reference>. The consecrating of them was the perfecting of them; Christ is said to be <hi type="italic">perfect</hi> or <hi type="italic">consecrated for evermore,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.28">Heb. vii. 28</reference>. Probably the phrase here is borrowed from the putting of the sacrifice into their hand, to be waved before the Lord, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.24">v. 24</reference>. But it intimates, [1.] That ministers have their hands full; they have no time to trifle, so great, so copious, so constant is their work. [2.] That they must have their hands filled. Of necessity <hi type="italic">they must have something to offer,</hi> and they cannot find it in themselves, it must be given them from above. They cannot fill the people's hearts unless God fill their hands; to him therefore they must go, and <hi type="italic">receive from his fulness.</hi> <div eID="gen2017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2018" type="x-p"/> (2.) The person to do it was Moses, by God's appointment. Though he was <hi type="italic">ordained for men,</hi> yet the people were not to consecrate him; Moses the <hi type="italic">servant of the Lord,</hi> and his agent herein, must do it. By God's special appointment he now did the priest's work, and therefore that which was the priest's part of the sacrifice was here ordered to be his, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.26">v. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen2018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2019" type="x-p"/> (3.) The place was at the <hi type="italic">door of the tabernacle of meeting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.29.4">v. 4</reference>. God was pleased to dwell in the tabernacle, the people attending in the courts, so that the door between the court and the tabernacle was the fittest place for those to be consecrated in who were to mediate between God and man, and to stand between both, and <hi type="italic">lay their hands</hi> (as it were) <hi type="italic">upon both.</hi> They were consecrated at the door, for they were to be door-keepers. <div eID="gen2019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2020" type="x-p"/> (4.) It was done with many ceremonies. <div eID="gen2020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2021" type="x-p"/> [1.] They were to be washed (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.4">v. 4</reference>), signifying that those must be clean who <hi type="italic">bear the vessels of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.52.11">Isa. lii. 11</reference>. Those that would <hi type="italic">perfect holiness</hi> must <hi type="italic">cleanse themselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2 Cor. vii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16-Isa.1.18">Isa. i. 16-18</reference>. They were now washed all over; but afterwards, when they went in to minister, they washed only their hands and feet (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.19">ch. xxx. 19</reference>); for <hi type="italic">he that is washed needs</hi> no more, <reference osisRef="John.13.10">John xiii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen2021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2022" type="x-p"/> [2.] They were to be clothed with the holy garments (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.5-Exod.29.6">v. 5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.9">9</reference>), to signify that it was not sufficient for them to put away the pollutions of sin, but they must put on the graces of the Spirit, be <hi type="italic">clothed with righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.9">Ps. cxxxii. 9</reference>. They must be girded, as men prepared and strengthened for their work; and they must be robed and crowned, as men that counted their work and office their true honour. <div eID="gen2022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2023" type="x-p"/> [3.] The high priest was to be anointed with the <hi type="italic">holy anointing oil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.7">v. 7</reference>), that the church might be filled and delighted with the sweet savour of his administrations (for <hi type="italic">ointment and perfume rejoice the heart</hi>), and in token of the pouring out of the Spirit upon him, to qualify him for his work. Brotherly love is compared to this oil with which Aaron was anointed, <reference osisRef="Ps.133.2">Ps. cxxxiii. 2</reference>. The inferior priests are said to be anointed (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.30">ch. xxx. 30</reference>), not on their heads, as the high priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.10">Lev. xxi. 10</reference>), the oil was only mingled with the blood that was sprinkled upon their garments. <div eID="gen2023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2024" type="x-p"/> [4.] Sacrifices were to be offered for them. The covenant of priesthood, as all other covenants, must be <hi type="italic">made by sacrifice.</hi> <div eID="gen2024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2025" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There must be a sin-offering, to make atonement for them, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.10-Exod.29.14">v. 10-14</reference>. The law made those priests that had infirmity, and therefore they must first offer for their own sin, before they could make atonement <hi type="italic">for the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.27-Heb.7.28">Heb. vii. 27, 28</reference>. They were to put their hand on the head of their sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.10">v. 10</reference>), confessing that they deserved to die for their own sin, and desiring that the killing of the beast might expiate their guilt, and be accepted as a vicarious satisfaction. It was used as other sin-offerings were; only, whereas the flesh of other sin-offerings was eaten by the priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.18">Lev. x. 18</reference>), in token of the priest's taking away the sin of the people, this was appointed to be all burnt without the camp (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.14">v. 14</reference>), to signify the imperfection of the legal dispensation (as the learned bishop Patrick notes); for the sins of the priests themselves could not be taken away by those sacrifices, but they must expect a better high priest and a better sacrifice. <div eID="gen2025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2026" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> There must be a burnt-offering, a ram wholly burnt, to the honour of God, in token of the dedication of themselves wholly to God and to his service, as living sacrifices, kindled with the fire and ascending in the flame of holy love, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.15-Exod.29.18">v. 15-18</reference>. The sin-offering must first be offered and then the burnt-offering; for, till guilt be removed, no acceptable service can be performed, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.7">Isa. vi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen2026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2027" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> There must be a peace-offering; it is called <hi type="italic">the ram of consecration,</hi> because there was more in this peculiar to the occasion than in the other two. In the burnt-offering God had the glory of their priesthood, in this they had the comfort of it; and, in token of a mutual covenant between God and them, 1. The blood of the sacrifice was divided between God and them (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.20-Exod.29.21">v. 20, 21</reference>); part of the blood was <hi type="italic">sprinkled upon the altar round about,</hi> and part put upon them, upon their bodies (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.20">v. 20</reference>), and upon their garments, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.21">v. 21</reference>. Thus the benefit of the expiation made by the sacrifice was applied and assured to them, and their whole selves from head to foot sanctified to the service of God. The blood was put upon the extreme parts of the body, to signify that it was all, as it were, enclosed and taken in for God, the tip of the ear and the great toe not excepted. We reckon that the blood and oil sprinkled upon garments spot and stain them; yet the holy oil, and the blood of the sacrifice, sprinkled upon their garments, must be looked upon as the greatest adorning imaginable to them, for they signified the blood of Christ, and the graces of the Spirit, which constitute and complete the beauty of holiness, and recommend us to God; we read of robes <hi type="italic">made white with the blood of the Lamb.</hi> 2. The <hi type="italic">flesh of the sacrifice,</hi> with the meat-offering annexed to it, was likewise divided between God and them, that (to speak with reverence) God and they might feast together, in token of friendship and fellowship. (1.) Part of it was to be first waved before the Lord, and then burnt upon the altar; part of the <hi type="italic">flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.22">v. 22</reference>), part of the <hi type="italic">bread,</hi> for bread and flesh must go together (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.23">v. 23</reference>); these were first put into the hands of Aaron to be waved to and fro, in token of their being offered to God (who, though unseen, yet compasses us round on every side), and then they were to be burnt upon the altar (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.24-Exod.29.25">v. 24, 25</reference>), for the altar was to devour God's part of the sacrifice. Thus God admitted Aaron and his sons to be his servants, and wait at his table, taking the mat of his altar from their hands. Here, in a parenthesis, as it were, comes in the law concerning the priests' part of the peace-offerings afterwards, the breast and shoulder, which were now divided; Moses had the breast, and the shoulder was burnt on the altar with God's part, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.26-Exod.29.28">v. 26-28</reference>. (2.) The other part, both of the flesh of the ram and of the bread, Aaron and his sons were to eat at the door of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.31-Exod.29.33">v. 31-33</reference>), to signify that he called them not only <hi type="italic">servants</hi> but <hi type="italic">friends,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.15">John xv. 15</reference>. He <hi type="italic">supped with them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">they with him.</hi> Their eating of the things wherewith <hi type="italic">the atonement was made</hi> signified their <hi type="italic">receiving the atonement,</hi> as the expression is (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">Rom. v. 11</reference>), their thankful acceptance of the benefit of it, and their joyful communion with God thereupon, which was the true intent and meaning of a feast upon a sacrifice. If any of it was left, it must be burnt, that it might not be in any danger of putrefying, and to show that it was an extraordinary peace-offering. <div eID="gen2027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2028" type="x-p"/> 2. The time that was to be spent in this consecration: <hi type="italic">Seven days shalt thou consecrate them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.29.35">v. 35</reference>. Though all the ceremonies were performed on the first day, yet, (1.) They were not to look upon their consecration as completed till the seven days' end, which put a solemnity upon their admission, and a distance between this and their former state, and obliged them to enter upon their work with a pause, giving them time to consider the weight and seriousness of it. This was to be observed in after-ages, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.30">v. 30</reference>. He that was to succeed Aaron in the high-priesthood must put on the holy garments seven days together, in token of a deliberate and gradual advance into his office, and that one sabbath might pass over him in his consecration. (2.) Every day of the seven, in this first consecration, a bullock was to be offered for a sin-offering (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.36">v. 36</reference>), which was to intimate to them, [1.] That it was of very great concern to them to get their sins pardoned, and that though atonement was made, and they had the comfort of it, yet they must still keep up a penitent sense of sin and often repeat the confession of it. [2.] That those sacrifices which were thus offered day by day to make atonement could not make the <hi type="italic">comers thereunto perfect,</hi> for then they would have ceased to be offered, as the apostle argues, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1-Heb.10.2">Heb. x. 1, 2</reference>. They must therefore expect the <hi type="italic">bringing in of a better hope.</hi> <div eID="gen2028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2029" type="x-p"/> 3. This consecration of the priests was a <hi type="italic">shadow of good things to come.</hi> (1.) Our Lord Jesus is the great high-priest of our profession, called of God to be so, consecrated for evermore, anointed with the Spirit above his fellows (whence he is called <hi type="italic">Messiah,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Christ</hi>), clothed with the holy garments, even with glory and beauty, sanctified by his own blood, not that of bullocks and rams (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb. ix. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">made perfect,</hi> or consecrated, <hi type="italic">through sufferings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. Thus in him this was a perpetual statute, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.9">v. 9</reference>. (2.) All believers are spiritual priests, to offer spiritual sacrifices (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1 Pet. ii. 5</reference>), washed in the blood of Christ, and so <hi type="italic">made to our God priests,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5-Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 5, 6</reference>. They also are clothed with the beauty of holiness, and have received the anointing, <reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1 John ii. 27</reference>. Their hands are filled with work, to which they must continually attend; and it is through Christ, the great sacrifice, that they are dedicated to this service. His blood <hi type="italic">sprinkled upon the conscience purges it from dead works, that they may,</hi> as priests, <hi type="italic">serve the living God.</hi> The Spirit of God (as Ainsworth notes) is called the <hi type="italic">finger of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.20">Luke xi. 20</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Matt.12.28">Matt. xii. 28</reference>), and by him the merit of Christ is effectually applied to our souls, as here Moses with his finger was to put the blood upon Aaron. It is likewise intimated that gospel ministers are to be solemnly set apart to the work of the ministry with great deliberation and seriousness both in the ordainers and in the ordained, as those that are to be employed in a great work and entrusted with a great charge. <div eID="gen2029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2030" type="x-p"/> II. The consecration of the altar, which seems to have been coincident with that of the priests, and the sin-offerings which were offered every day for seven days together had reference to the altar as well as the priests, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.36-Exod.29.37">v. 36, 37</reference>. An <hi type="italic">atonement</hi> was <hi type="italic">made for the altar.</hi> Though that was not a subject capable of sin, nor, having never yet been used, could it be said to be polluted with the sins of the people, yet, since the fall, there can be no sanctification to God but there must first be <hi type="italic">an atonement for sin,</hi> which renders us both unworthy and unfit to be employed for God. The altar was also <hi type="italic">sanctified,</hi> not only set apart itself to a sacred use, but made so holy as to <hi type="italic">sanctify the gifts</hi> that were offered upon it, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.19">Matt. xxiii. 19</reference>. Christ is our altar; for our sakes he sanctified himself, that we and our performances might be sanctified and recommended to God, <reference osisRef="John.17.19">John xvii. 19</reference>.
entries.74d309899f425ad97982b8926b5fd8fb5ed10cbe: <div eID="gen2030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2031" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> Now this <hi type="italic">is that</hi> which thou shalt offer upon the altar; two lambs of the first year day by day continually. <hi type="super">39</hi> The one lamb thou shalt offer in the morning; and the other lamb thou shalt offer at even: <hi type="super">40</hi> And with the one lamb a tenth deal of flour mingled with the fourth part of an hin of beaten oil; and the fourth part of an hin of wine <hi type="italic">for</hi> a drink offering. <hi type="super">41</hi> And the other lamb thou shalt offer at even, and shalt do thereto according to the meat offering of the morning, and according to the drink offering thereof, for a sweet savour, an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">42</hi> <hi type="italic">This shall be</hi> a continual burnt offering throughout your generations <hi type="italic">at</hi> the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : where I will meet you, to speak there unto thee. <hi type="super">43</hi> And there I will meet with the children of Israel, and <hi type="italic">the tabernacle</hi> shall be sanctified by my glory. <hi type="super">44</hi> And I will sanctify the tabernacle of the congregation, and the altar: I will sanctify also both Aaron and his sons, to minister to me in the priest's office. <hi type="super">45</hi> And I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will be their God. 46 And they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, that brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, that I may dwell among them: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <div eID="gen2031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2032" type="x-p"/> In this paragraph we have, <div eID="gen2032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2033" type="x-p"/> I. The daily service appointed. A lamb was to be offered upon the altar every morning, and a lamb every evening, each with a meat-offering, both made by fire, as a <hi type="italic">continual burnt-offering throughout their generations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.41">v. 38-41</reference>. Whether there were any other sacrifices to be offered or not, these were sure to be offered, at the public charge, for the benefit and comfort of all Israel, to make atonement for their daily sins, and to be an acknowledgement to God of their daily mercies. This was that which <hi type="italic">the duty of every day required.</hi> The taking away of this daily sacrifice by Antiochus, for so many evenings and mornings, was that great calamity of the church which was foretold, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.11">Dan. viii. 11</reference>. Note, 1. This typified the continual intercession which Christ ever lives to make, in virtue of his satisfaction, for the continual sanctification of his church: though he offered himself <hi type="italic">once for all,</hi> yet that one offering thus becomes a continual offering. 2. This teaches us to offer up to God the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise every day, morning and evening, in humble acknowledgement of our dependence upon him and our obligations to him. Our daily devotions must be looked upon as the most needful of our daily works and the most pleasant of our daily comforts. Whatever business we have, this must never be omitted, either morning or evening; prayer-time must be kept up as duly as meat-time. The daily sacrifices were as the daily meals in God's house, and therefore they were always attended with bread and wine. Those starve their own souls that keep not up a constant attendance on the throne of grace. <div eID="gen2033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2034" type="x-p"/> II. Great and precious promises made of God's favour to Israel, and the tokens of his special presence with them, while they thus kept up his institutions among them. He speaks as one well pleased with the appointment of the daily sacrifice; for, before he proceeds to the other appointments that follow, he interposes these promises. It is constancy in religion that brings in the comfort of it. He promises, 1. That he would keep up communion with them; that he would not only meet Moses, and speak to him, but that he would <hi type="italic">meet the children of Israel,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.43">v. 43</reference>), to accept the daily sacrifices offered up on their behalf. Note, God will not fail to give those the meeting who diligently and conscientiously attend upon him in the ordinances of his own appointment. 2. That he would own his own institutions, the tabernacle, the altar, the priesthood (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.43-Exod.29.44">v. 43, 44</reference>); he would take possession of that which was consecrated to him. Note, What is sanctified to the glory of God shall be sanctified by his glory. If we do our part, God will do his, and will mark and fit that for himself which is in sincerity given up to him. 3. That he would reside among them as God in covenant with them, and would give them sure and comfortable tokens of his peculiar favour to them, and his special presence with them (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.45-Exod.29.46">v. 45, 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will dwell among the children of Israel.</hi> Note, Where God sets up the tabernacle of his ordinances he will himself dwell. <hi type="italic">Lo, I am with you always,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>. Those that abide in God's house shall have God to abide with them. <hi type="italic">I will be their God, and they shall know</hi> that I am so. Note, Those are truly happy that have a covenant-interest in God as theirs and the comfortable evidence of that interest. If we have this, we have enough, and need no more to make us happy.  <chapter eID="Exod.29"/> <div eID="gen2034" type="x-p"/>

entries.130881011d6d763251a837016798b82b1de5a54f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv885"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.29.1-Exod.29.35">Ex 29:1-35</reference>. Consecrating the Priests and the Altar.</title> <div sID="gen1227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv885"/><hi type="bold">1. hallow them, to minister unto me in the priest's office--</hi>The act of inaugurating the priests was accompanied by ceremonial solemnities well calculated not only to lead the people to entertain exalted views of the office, but to impress those functionaries themselves with a profound sense of its magnitude and importance. In short, they were taught to know that the service was for them as well as for the people; and every time they engaged in a new performance of their duties, they were reminded of their personal interest in the worship, by being obliged to offer for themselves, before they were qualified to offer as the representatives of the people.<div eID="gen1227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this is the thing that thou shalt do--</hi>Steps are taken at the beginning of a society, which would not be repeated when the social machine was in full motion; and Moses, at the opening of the tabernacle, was employed to discharge functions which in later periods would have been regarded as sacrilege and punished with instant death. But he acted under the special directions of God. <div eID="gen1228" type="x-p"/>
entries.a97adbe2cc28f0b329c8934326b3ab60c0496376: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv886"/><div sID="gen1229" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv886"/><hi type="bold">4-9. Aaron and his sons thou shalt bring unto the door of the tabernacle--</hi>as occupying the intermediate space between the court where the people stood, and the dwelling-place of Israel's king, and therefore the fittest spot for the priests being duly prepared for entrance, and the people witnessing the ceremony of inauguration.<div eID="gen1229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wash them with water. And ... take the garments--</hi>The manner in which these parts of the ceremonial were performed is minutely described, and in discovering their symbolical import, which indeed, is sufficiently plain and obvious, we have inspired authority to guide us. It signified the necessity and importance of moral purity or holiness (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.11">Is 52:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.10">Joh 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2Co 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>). In like manner, the investiture with the holy garments signified their being clothed with righteousness (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Re 19:8</reference>) and equipped as men active and well-prepared for the service of God; the anointing the high priest with oil denoted that he was to be filled with the influences of the Spirit, for the edification and delight of the church (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.7">Le 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Is 61:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1Jo 2:27</reference>), and as he was officially a type of Christ (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.26">He 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.34">Joh 3:34</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Matt.3.16">Mt 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">11:29</reference>). <div eID="gen1230" type="x-p"/>
entries.c855f7bcee3e9d0101e89e0a273adac282e8d5e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv887"/><div sID="gen1231" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv887"/><hi type="bold">10-22. And thou shalt cause a bullock to be brought before the tabernacle--</hi>This part of the ceremonial consisted of three sacrifices: <hi type="bold">(1) The sacrifice of a bullock, as a sin offering; and in rendering it, the priest was directed to put his hand upon the head of his sacrifice, expressing by that act a consciousness of personal guilt, and a wish that it might be accepted as a vicarious satisfaction. (2) The sacrifice of a ram as a burnt offering (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.15-Exod.29.18">Ex 29:15-18</reference>). The ram was to be wholly burnt, in token of the priest's dedication of himself to God and His service. The sin offering was first to be presented, and then the burnt offering; for until guilt be removed, no acceptable service can be performed. (3) There was to be a peace offering, called "the ram of consecration" (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.19-Exod.29.22">Ex 29:19-22</reference>). And there was a marked peculiarity in the manner in which this other ram was to be disposed of. The former was for the glory of God--</hi>this was for the comfort of the priest himself; and as a sign of a mutual covenant being ratified, the blood of the sacrifice was divided--part sprinkled on the altar round about, and part upon the persons and garments of the priests. Nay, the blood was, by a singular act, directed to be put upon the extremities of the body, thereby signifying that the benefits of the atonement would be applied to the whole nature of man. Moreover, the flesh of this sacrifice was to be divided, as it were, between God and the priest--part of it to be put into his hand to be waved up and down, in token of its being offered to God, and then it was to be burnt upon the altar; the other part was to be eaten by the priests at the door of the tabernacle--that feast being a symbol of communion or fellowship with God. These ceremonies, performed in the order described, showed the qualifications necessary for the priests. (See <reference osisRef="Heb.7.26">He 7:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.14">10:14</reference>). <div eID="gen1231" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ae9f3657b3fe1d3b423177ca9a2ed4370feafbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv888"/><div sID="gen1232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv888"/><hi type="bold">35. seven days shalt thou consecrate them--</hi>The renewal of these ceremonies on the return of every day in the seven, with the intervention of a Sabbath, was a wise preparatory arrangement, in order to afford a sufficient interval for calm and devout reflection (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.1">He 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">10:1</reference>).<div eID="gen1232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1233" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Exod.29.36">Ex 29:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">37</reference>. Consecration of the Altar. <div eID="gen1233" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ed4e727bfb3a79c52b9300322d99a1b58643b6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv889"/><div sID="gen1234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv889"/><hi type="bold">36. and thou shalt cleanse the altar--</hi>The phrase, "when thou hast made an atonement for it," should be, upon it; and the purport of the direction is, that during all the time they were engaged as above from day to day in offering the appointed sacrifices, the greatest care was to be taken to keep the altar properly cleansed--to remove the ashes, and sprinkle it with the prescribed unction that, at the conclusion of the whole ceremonial, the altar itself should be consecrated as much as the ministers who were to officiate at it (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.19">Mt 23:19</reference>). It was thenceforth associated with the services of religion. <div eID="gen1234" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f23904c154649bd267c726ead1d0b95d97f55dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv890"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.46">Ex 29:38-46</reference>. Institution of Daily Service.</title> <div sID="gen1235" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv890"/><hi type="bold">38. two lambs of the first year day by day continually--</hi>The sacred preliminaries being completed, Moses was instructed in the end or design to which these preparations were subservient, namely, the worship of God; and hence the institution of the morning and evening sacrifice. The institution was so imperative, that in no circumstances was this daily oblation to be dispensed with; and the due observance of it would secure the oft-promised grace and blessing of their heavenly King. <chapter eID="Exod.29"/>

entries.b303479b815ffa1988d4d957c235f49d8a61abc1: <div eID="gen3814" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen3815" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3816" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3816" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3815" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3817" type="x-p"/> Ceremonies to be used in consecrating Aaron and his sons, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.1-Exo.29.3">Exo 29:1-3</reference>. They are to be washed, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.4">Exo 29:4</reference>. Aaron is to be clothed with the holy vestments, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.5">Exo 29:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.6">Exo 29:6</reference>; to be anointed, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.7">Exo 29:7</reference>. His sons to be clothed and girded, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.8">Exo 29:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.9">Exo 29:9</reference>. They are to offer a bullock for a sin-offering, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.10-Exo.29.14">Exo 29:10-14</reference>; and a ram for a burnt-offering, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.15-Exo.29.18">Exo 29:15-18</reference>; and a second ram for a consecration-offering, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.19-Exo.29.22">Exo 29:19-22</reference>. A loaf, a cake, and a wafer or thin cake, for a wave-offering, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.23-Exo.29.25">Exo 29:23-25</reference>. The breast of the wave-offering and the shoulder of the heave-offering to be sanctified, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.26-Exo.29.28">Exo 29:26-28</reference>. Aaron's vestments to descend to his son, who shall succeed him, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.29">Exo 29:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.30">Exo 29:30</reference>. Aaron and his sons to eat the flesh of the ram of consecration, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.31">Exo 29:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.32">Exo 29:32</reference>. No stranger to eat of it, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.33">Exo 29:33</reference>. Nothing of it to be left till the morning, but to be burnt with fire, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.34">Exo 29:34</reference>. Seven days to be employed in consecrating Aaron and his sons, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.35-Exo.29.37">Exo 29:35-37</reference>. Two lambs, one for the morning and the other for the evening sacrifice, to be offered continually, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.38-Exo.29.42">Exo 29:38-42</reference>. God promises to sanctify Israel with his glory, and to dwell among them, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.43-Exo.29.46">Exo 29:43-46</reference>. <div eID="gen3817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen3818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3819" type="x-p"/> Take one young bullock - This consecration did not take place till after the erection of the tabernacle. See <reference osisRef="Lev.8.9-Lev.8.14">Lev 8:9-14</reference>.
entries.67b9b7071442f5a680941777b176ed567ae41ff0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen3819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3820" type="x-p"/> Unleavened bread - Three kinds of bread as to its form are mentioned here, but all unleavened: <div eID="gen3820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3821" type="x-p"/> 1. מצות matstsoth, unleavened bread, no matter in what shape. See <reference osisRef="Exo.12.8">Exo 12:8</reference>. <div eID="gen3821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3822" type="x-p"/> 2. חלת challoth, cakes, pricked or perforated, as the root implies. <div eID="gen3822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3823" type="x-p"/> 3. רקיקי rekikey, an exceeding thin cake, from רק rak, to be attenuated, properly enough translated wafer. The manner in which these were prepared is sufficiently plain from the text, and probably these were the principal forms in which flour was prepared for household use during their stay in the wilderness. <div eID="gen3823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3824" type="x-p"/> These were all waved before the Lord, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.24">Exo 29:24</reference>, as an acknowledgment that the bread that sustains the body, as well as the mercy which saves the soul, comes from God alone.
entries.cc0c29363c4d28da977fc4e5a5785b01b3d9151e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen3824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3825" type="x-p"/> Thou - shalt wash them - This was done emblematically, to signify that they were to put away all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, and perfect holiness in the fear of God; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2Cor 7:1</reference>.
entries.ca106f0037bc9133565d8395df70d407df1ca5da: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen3825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3826" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt take the garments - As most offices of spiritual and secular dignity had appropriate habits and insignia, hence, when a person was appointed to an office and habited for the purpose, he was said to be invested with that office, from in, used intensively, and vestio, I clothe, because he was then clothed with the vestments peculiar to that office.
entries.247f8e05de82dc079aaf2ec20255f11cdf618d30: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen3826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3827" type="x-p"/> Then shalt thou take the anointing oil - It appears, from <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa 61:1</reference>, that anointing with oil, in consecrating a person to any important office, whether civil or religious, was considered as an emblem of the communication of the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit. This ceremony was used on three occasions, viz., the installation of prophets, priests, and kings, into their respective offices. But why should such an anointing be deemed necessary? Because the common sense of men taught them that all good, whether spiritual or secular, must come from God, its origin and cause. Hence it was taken for granted, <div eID="gen3827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3828" type="x-p"/> 1. That no man could foretell events unless inspired by the Spirit of God. And therefore the prophet was anointed, to signify the communication of the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge. <div eID="gen3828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3829" type="x-p"/> 2. That no person could offer an acceptable sacrifice to God for the sins of men, or profitably minister in holy things, unless enlightened, influenced, and directed by the Spirit of grace and holiness. Hence the priest was anointed, to signify his being Divinely qualified for the due performance of his sacred functions. <div eID="gen3829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3830" type="x-p"/> 3. That no man could enact just and equitable laws, which should have the prosperity of the community and the welfare of the individual continually in view, or could use the power confided to him only for the suppression of vice and the encouragement of virtue, but that man who was ever under the inspiration of the Almighty. <div eID="gen3830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3831" type="x-p"/> Hence kings were inaugurated by anointing with oil. Two of these officers only exist in all civilized nations, the sacerdotal and regal; and in some countries the priest and king are still consecrated by anointing. In the Hebrew language משח mashach signifies to anoint, and משיח mashiach, the anointed person. But as no man was ever dignified by holding the three offices, so no person ever had the title mashiach, the anointed one, but Jesus the Christ. He alone is King of kings and Lord of lords: the king who governs the universe, and rules in the hearts of his followers; the prophet, to instruct men in the way wherein they should go; and the great high priest, to make atonement for their sins. Hence he is called the Messias, a corruption of the word המשיח hammashiach, The anointed One, in Hebrew; which gave birth to ὁ Χριστος, ho Christos, which has precisely the same signification in Greek. Of him, Melchizedek, Abraham, Aaron, David, and others were illustrious types. But none of these had the title of The Messiah, or The Anointed of God. This does, and ever will, belong exclusively to Jesus the Christ.
entries.7ae83fc3a48b5159b203ef700ac04bfdd97b62a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen3831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3832" type="x-p"/> Shall put their hands upon the head of the bullock - By this rite the animal was consecrated to God, and was then proper to be offered in sacrifice. Imposition of hands also signified that they offered the life of this animal as an atonement for their sins, and to redeem their lives from that death which, through their sinfulness, they had deserved. In the case of the sin-offering and trespass-offering, the person who brought the sacrifice placed his hands on the head of the animal between the horns, and confessed his sin over the sin-offering, and his trespass over the trespass-offering, saying, "I have sinned, I have done iniquity; I have trespassed, and have done thus and thus; and do return by repentance before thee, and with this I make atonement." Then the animal was considered as vicariously bearing the sins of the person who brought it - <reference osisRef="Exo.29.14">Exo 29:14</reference>
entries.5dc59f6a5eb1a678b4fed1fa036ba3691724f3a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen3832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3833" type="x-p"/> It is a sin-offering - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>; See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.13.13">Gen 13:13</reference>; See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.1">Lev 7:1</reference>, etc.
entries.2f68fe480351fc1ddcdc37b8e9b3d30182ee6538: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen3833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3834" type="x-p"/> It is a burnt-offering - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.1">Lev 7:1</reference>, etc.
entries.fa4927263bd7e86f81fbc77684226702f5e64d45: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen3834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3835" type="x-p"/> The other ram - There were two rams brought on this occasion: one was for a burnt-offering, and was to be entirely consumed; the other was the ram of consecration, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.22">Exo 29:22</reference>, איל מלאים eil milluim, the ram of filling up, because when a person was dedicated or consecrated to God, his hands were filled with some particular offering proper for the occasion, which he presented to God. Hence the word consecration signifies the filling up or filling the hands, some part of the sacrifice being put into the hands of such persons, denoting thereby that they had now a right to offer sacrifices and oblations to God. It seems in reference to this ancient mode of consecration, that in the Church of England, when a person is ordained priest, a Bible is put into his hands with these words, "Take thou authority to preach the word of God, etc. The filling the hands refers also to the presents which, in the eastern countries, every inferior was obliged to bring when brought into the presence of a superior. Thus the sacrifice was considered, not only as an atonement for sin, but also as a means of approach and as a present to Jehovah.
entries.5980eee06fc4750f89176e4ca85e42ae2fbc195d: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen3835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3836" type="x-p"/> Take of his blood - The putting the blood of the sacrifice on the tip of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the great toe of the right foot, was doubtless intended to signify that they should dedicate all their faculties and powers to the service of God; their ears to the hearing and study of his law, their hands to diligence in the sacred ministry and to all acts of obedience, and their feet to walking in the way of God's precepts. And this sprinkling appears to have been used to teach them that they could neither hear, work, nor walk profitably, uprightly, and well-pleasing in the sight of God, without this application of the blood of the sacrifice. And as the blood of rams, bulls, and goats, could never take away sin, does not this prove to us that something infinitely better is shadowed out, and that we can do nothing holy and pure in the sight of a just and holy God, but through the blood of atonement? See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.30.20">Exo 30:20</reference>.
entries.c7475276bde965b7171b40c3d5f912c50b2fdfcd: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen3836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3837" type="x-p"/> The fat and the rump - The rump or tail of some of the eastern sheep is the best part of the animal, and is counted a great delicacy. They are also very large, some of them weighing from twelve to forty pounds' weight; "so that the owners," says Mr. Ludolf, in his History of Ethiopia, "are obliged to tie a little cart behind them, whereon they put the tail of the sheep, as well for the convenience of carriage, and to ease the poor creature, as to preserve the wool from dirt, and the tail from being torn among the bushes and stones." An engraving of this kind of sheep, his tall, cart, etc., may be seen at p. 53 of the above work.
entries.12ec838e1c2f6958eca9965004efd14e63362ca5: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen3837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3838" type="x-p"/> And one loaf of bread - The bread of different kinds, (see Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.2">Exo 29:2</reference> (note)), in this offering, seems to have been intended as a minchah, or offering of grateful acknowledgment for providential blessings. The essence of worship consisted in acknowledging God, <div eID="gen3838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3839" type="x-p"/> 1. As the Creator, Governor, and Preserver of all things, and the Dispenser of every good and perfect gift. <div eID="gen3839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3840" type="x-p"/> 2. As the Judge of men, the Punisher of sin, and he who alone could pardon it. <div eID="gen3840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3841" type="x-p"/> The minchahs, heave-offerings, wave-offerings, and thank-offerings, referred to the first point. The burnt-offerings, sin-offerings, and sacrifices in general, referred to the second.
entries.9c23c233950b955d75fbe64dbe64f92451fa78b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen3841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3842" type="x-p"/> For a wave-offering - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.1">Lev 7:1</reference> etc., where an ample account of all the offerings, sacrifices, etc., under the Mosaic dispensation, and the reference they bore to the great sacrifice offered by Christ, is given in detail.
entries.c2960aed8c742eaa174b68cc9100371416ac41d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen3842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3843" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt receive them of their hands - Aaron and his sons are here considered merely as any common persons bringing an offering to God, and not having, as yet, any authority to present it themselves, but through the medium of a priest. Moses, therefore, was now to Aaron and his sons what they were afterwards to the children of Israel; and as the minister of God he now consecrates them to the sacred office, and presents their offerings to Jehovah.
entries.233ceaebe6cc80b95e484c5bfef365ba4e37f741: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen3843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3844" type="x-p"/> The breast of the wave-offering, and the shoulder of the heave-offering - As the wave-offering was agitated to and fro, and the heave-offering up and down, some have conceived that this twofold action represented the figure of the cross, on which the great Peace-offering between God and man was offered in the personal sacrifice of our blessed Redeemer. Had we authority for this conjecture, it would certainly cast much light on the meaning and intention of these offerings; and when the intelligent reader is informed that one of the most judicious critics in the whole republic of letters is the author of this conjecture, viz., Houbigant, he will treat it with respect. I shall here produce his own words on this verse: <div eID="gen3844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3845" type="x-p"/> Hic distinguuntur, תנופה et תרומה, ut ejusdem oblationis caeremoniae duae. In תנופה significatur, moveri oblatam victimam huc et illuc, ad dextram et ad sinistram. In תרומה sursum tolli, et sublatam rursus deprimi; nam pluribus vicibus id fiebat. Rem sic interpretantur Judaei; et Christianos docent, quanquam id non agentes, sic adumbrari eam crucem, in quam generis humani victima illa pacifica sublata est, quam veteres victimae omnes praenunciabant. "The heave-offering and wave-offering, as two ceremonies in the same oblation, are here distinguished. The wave-offering implies that the victim was moved hither and thither, to the right hand and to the left; the heave-offering was lifted up and down, and this was done several times. In this way the Jews explain these things, and teach the Christians, that by these acts the cross was adumbrated, upon which that Peace-offering of the human race was lifted up which was prefigured by all the ancient victims." <div eID="gen3845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3846" type="x-p"/> The breast and the shoulder, thus waved and heaved, were by this consecration appointed to be the priests' portion for ever; and this, as Mr. Ainsworth piously remarks, "taught the priests how, with all their heart and all their strength, they should give themselves unto the service of the Lord in his Church." Moses, as priest, received on this occasion the breast and the shoulder, which became afterwards the portion of the priests; see <reference osisRef="Exo.29.28">Exo 29:28</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.7.34">Lev 7:34</reference>. It is worthy of remark, that although Moses himself had no consecration to the sacerdotal office, yet he acts here as high priest, consecrates a high priest, and receives the breast and the shoulder, which were the priests' portion! But Moses was an extraordinary messenger, and derived his authority, without the medium of rites or ceremonies, immediately from God himself. It does not appear that Christ either baptized the twelve apostles, or ordained them by imposition of hands; yet, from his own infinite sufficiency, he gave them authority both to baptize, and to lay on hands, in appointing others to the work of the sacred ministry. <reference osisRef="Exo.29.29">Exo 29:29</reference>
entries.67c4cf4c70e67fe8e21e39db96030d41a2004d1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen3846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3847" type="x-p"/> The holy garments - shall be his son's after him - These garments were to descend from father to son, and no new garments were to be made.
entries.71b816f2effac17110c32a6628bbfe0aee722b3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen3847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3848" type="x-p"/> Seven days - The priest in his consecration was to abide seven days and nights at the door of the tabernacle, keeping the Lord's watch. See <reference osisRef="Lev.8.33">Lev 8:33</reference>, etc. The number seven is what is called among the Hebrews a number of perfection; and it is often used to denote the completion, accomplishment, fullness, or perfection of a thing, as this period contained the whole course of that time in which God created the world, and appointed the day of rest. As this act of consecration lasted seven days, it signified a perfect consecration: and intimated to the priest that his whole body and soul, his time and talents, should be devoted to the service of God and his people. <div eID="gen3848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3849" type="x-p"/> The number seven, which was a sacred number among the Hebrews, was conveyed from them down to the Greeks by means of the Egyptian philosophy, from which they borrowed most of their mysteries; and it is most likely that the opinion which the Greeks give is the same that the original framers of the idea had. That there was some mystical idea attached to it, is evident from its being made the number of perfection among the Hebrews. Philo and Josephus say that the Essenes, an ancient sect of the Jews, held it sacred "because it results from the side of a square added to those of a triangle." But what meaning does this convey? A triangle, or triad, according to the Pythagoreans, who borrowed their systems from the Egyptians, who borrowed from the Jews, was the emblem of wisdom, as consisting of beginning (Monad), middle (Duad), and end (Triad itself); so wisdom consists of three parts - experience of the past, attention to the present, and judgment of the future. It is also the most penetrating of all forms, as being the shape of the wedge; and indestructibility is essential to it, as a triangle can never be destroyed. From those three properties it was the emblem of spirit. The square, solid, and tetrad, by the same system were interchangeable signs. Now a square is the representation of a solid or matter, and thus the number seven contains within itself the properties of both the triangle or solid, and the square or tetrad, i.e., is all emblem of body and spirit; comprehends both the intellectual and natural world; embraces the idea of God, the chief of spirits or essences; and all nature, the result of his power; thus a very fit emblem of perfection. It is perhaps in this way that we must explain what Cicero, Tusc. Quest., lib. i., cap. 10, says of the number seven, where he calls it the knot and cement of all things; as being that by which the natural and spiritual world are comprehended in one idea. Thus the ancient philosophers spoke of numbers, themselves being the best judges of their own meaning.
entries.3389d8588388874aa77774a07fee8c42b9b3ef5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen3849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3850" type="x-p"/> But a stranger shall not eat thereof - That is, no person who was not of the family of Aaron - no Israelite, and not even a Levite.
entries.819ec2c84cb296de26a2df8bd42a6fbd3eb4a9e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen3850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3851" type="x-p"/> Burn the remainder with fire - Common, voluntary, and peace-offerings, might be eaten even on the second day; see <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.5">Lev 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.6">Lev 19:6</reference>. But this being a peculiar consecration, in order to qualify a person to offer sacrifices for sin, like that great sacrifice, the paschal lamb, that typified the atonement made by Christ, none of it was to be left till the morning lest putrefaction should commence, which would be utterly improper in a sacrifice that was to make expiation for sin, and bring the soul into a state of holiness and perfection with God. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.10">Exo 12:10</reference>.
entries.9634fba252d7c3166db8b15dc35b10de9a7adb72: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen3851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3852" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt cleanse the altar - The altar was to be sanctified for seven days; and it is likely that on each day, previously to the consecration service, the altar was wiped clean, and the former day's ashes, etc., removed.
entries.b7c495137fd3731a1aee60a18ab8dab8e1b509ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen3852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3853" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever touches the altar shall be holy - To this our Lord refers <reference osisRef="Mat.23.19">Mat 23:19</reference>, where he says the altar sanctifies the gift; and this may be understood as implying that whatever was laid on the altar became the Lord's property, and must be wholly devoted to sacred uses, for in no other sense could such things be sanctified by touching the altar.
entries.dbca9ed06b6246d52333af018d0d9e8d2a41a4f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen3853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3854" type="x-p"/> One lamb thou shalt offer in the morning - These two lambs, one in the morning, and the other in the evening, were generally termed the morning and evening daily sacrifices, and were offered from the time of their settlement in the promised land to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans. The use of these sacrifices according to the Jews was this: "The morning sacrifice made atonement for the sins committed in the night, and the evening sacrifice expiated the sins committed during the day."
entries.cf7a185d2e30e96c0d0b086f7649f8e4f55a4f82: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen3854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3855" type="x-p"/> A tenth deal of flour - Deal signifies a part, from the Anglo-Saxon word, to divide; hence, a part, a portion taken from the whole. From <reference osisRef="Num.28.5">Num 28:5</reference> we learn that this tenth deal was the tenth part of an ephah, which constituted what is called an omer. See <reference osisRef="Exo.16.36">Exo 16:36</reference>; and see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.16.16">Exo 16:16</reference> of the same chapter, where an account is given of different measures of capacity among the Hebrews. The omer contained about three quarts English. <div eID="gen3855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3856" type="x-p"/> The fourth part of a hin - The hin contained one gallon and two pints. The fourth part of this was about one quart and a half of a pint. <div eID="gen3856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3857" type="x-p"/> Drink-offering - A libation poured out before the Lord. See its meaning, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.1">Lev 7:1</reference>, etc.
entries.d03244dad01a96cf6b62893f1af4af2a4337ada5: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen3857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3858" type="x-p"/> There I will meet with the children of Israel - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.25.22">Exo 25:22</reference>.
entries.ccd1ec8468ef3ae4b894e6839fe023c8f975de29: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen3858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3859" type="x-p"/> I will sanctify - both Aaron and his sons - So we find the sanctification by Moses according to the Divine institution was only symbolical; and that Aaron and his sons must be sanctified, i.e., made holy, by God himself before they could officiate in holy things. From this, as well as from many other things mentioned in the sacred writings, we may safely infer that no designation by man only is sufficient to qualify any person to fill the office of a minister of the sanctuary. The approbation and consecration of man have both their propriety and use, but must never be made substitutes for the unction and inspiration of the Almighty. Let holy men ordain, but let God sanctify; then we may expect that his Church shall be built up on its most holy faith.
entries.0dabfa9f3c854afa912f77aad3cccf2adc9a51da: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen3859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3860" type="x-p"/> I will dwell among the children of Israel - This is the great charter of the people of God, both under the Old and New Testaments; see <reference osisRef="Exo.25.8">Exo 25:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">Lev 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">Lev 26:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Cor 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Rev 21:3</reference>. God dwells Among them: he is ever to be found in his Church to enlighten, quicken, comfort, and support it; to dispense the light of life by the preaching of his word, and the influences of his Spirit for the conviction and conversion of sinners. And he dwells In those who believe; and this is the very tenor of the New Covenant which God promised to make with the house of Israel; see <reference osisRef="Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34">Jer 31:31-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.37.24-Eze.37.28">Eze 37:24-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.7-Heb.8.12">Heb 8:7-12</reference>; and <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Cor 6:16</reference>. And because God had promised to dwell in all his genuine followers, hence the frequent reference to this covenant and its privileges in the New Testament. And hence it is so frequently and strongly asserted that every believer is a habitation of God through the Spirit, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.22">Eph 2:22</reference>. That the Spirit of God witnesses with their spirits that they are the children of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.16">Rom 8:16</reference>. That the Spirit of Christ in their hearts enables them to call God their Father, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal 4:6</reference>. And that if any man have not this Spirit, he is none of his, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.9">Rom 8:9</reference>, etc. And hence St. Paul states this to be the sum and substance of apostolical preaching, and the riches of the glory of the mystery of the Gospel among the Gentiles, viz., Christ In you the hope of glory; whom, says he, we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect In Christ Jesus; <reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>.
entries.0ca7bb6f14c4ca3079cd8b4cb773a38f36ae840b: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen3860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3861" type="x-p"/> And they shall know that I am the Lord their God - That is, They shall acknowledge God, and their infinite obligations to him. In a multitude of places in Scripture the word know should be thus understood. <div eID="gen3861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3862" type="x-p"/> That I may dwell among them - For without this acknowledgment and consequent dependence on and gratitude and obedience to God, they could not expect him to dwell among them. <div eID="gen3862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3863" type="x-p"/> By dwelling among the people God shows that he would be a continual resident in their houses and in their hearts; that he would be their God - the sole object of their religious worship, to whom they should turn and on whom they should trust in all difficulties and distresses; and that he would be to them all that the Creator could be to his creatures. That in consequence they should have a full conviction of his presence and blessing, and a consciousness that He was their God, and that they were his people. Thus then God dwells among men that they may know him; and they must know him that he may continue to dwell among them. He who does not experimentally know God, cannot have him as an indwelling Savior; and he who does not continue to know - to acknowledge, love, and obey him, cannot retain him as his Preserver and Sanctifier. From the beginning of the world, the salvation of the souls of men necessarily implied the indwelling influences of God. Reader, hast thou this salvation? This alone will support thee in all thy travels in this wilderness, comfort thee in death, and give thee boldness in the day of judgment. "He," says an old writer, "who has pardon may look his judge in the face."  <chapter eID="Exod.29"/> <div eID="gen3863" type="x-p"/>

entries.fc3ff43572e9989e5f82a0085354deb3229966ef: <reference osisRef="Exod.29.1-Exod.29.37">Exo 29:1-37</reference> <div eID="gen1053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1054" type="x-p"/> Consecration of Aaron and his Sons through the anointing of their persons and the offering of sacrifices, the directions for which form the subject of vv. 1-35. This can only be fully understood in connection with the sacrificial law contained in Lev 1-7. It will be more advisable therefore to defer the examination of this ceremony till we come to Lev 8, where the consecration itself is described. The same may also be said of the expiation and anointing of the altar, which are commanded in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.36">Exo 29:36</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">Exo 29:37</reference>, and carried out in Lev 8:11. <div eID="gen1054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1055" type="x-p"/> The Daily Burnt-Offering, Meat-Offering, and Drink-Offering. - The directions concerning these are attached to the instructions for the consecration of the priests, because these sacrifices commenced immediately after the completion of the tabernacle, and, like the shew-bread (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.30">Exo 25:30</reference>), the daily trimming of the lamps (<reference osisRef="Exod.27.20-Exod.27.21">Exo 27:20-21</reference>), and the daily incense-offering (Exo 30:7.), were most intimately connected with the erection of the sanctuary.
entries.8ad7fa473424a276ff638682ebba4c481621ba67: <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.40">Exo 29:38-40</reference> <div eID="gen1055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1056" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And this is what thou shalt make</hi> (offer) <hi type="italic">upon the altar; yearling lambs two a day continually,</hi>” one in the morning, the other between the two evenings (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.12.6">Exo 12:6</reference>); to every one a meat-offering (<hi type="italic">minchah</hi>) of a tenth of fine wheaten flour (<hi type="italic">soleth</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Lev 2:1</reference>), mixed with a quarter of a hin of beaten oil (<hi type="italic">cathith</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.27.20">Exo 27:20</reference>), and a drink-offering (<hi type="italic">nesek</hi>) of a quarter of a hin of wine. עשּׂרן (a tenth) is equivalent to האיפה עשׂירית, the tenth part of an ephah (Num 28:5), or 198-5 Parisian cubic inches according to Bertheau’s measurement. <hi type="italic">Thenius</hi>, however, sets it down at 101-4 inches, whilst the Rabbins reckon it as equivalent to 43 hen’s eggs of average size, i.e., somewhat more than 2 1/4 lbs. A hin (a word of Egyptian origin) is 330-9 inches according to <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>, 168-9 according to Thenius, or 72 eggs, so that a quarter of a hin would be 18 eggs.
entries.10db77a78153c87205fce27dca71b2aa38e2d2a8: <reference osisRef="Exod.29.41-Exod.29.46">Exo 29:41-46</reference> להּ is to be understood <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi> as referring to עולה. The daily morning and evening sacrifices were to be “for a sweet savour, a firing unto Jehovah” (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.1.9">Lev 1:9</reference>). In these Israel was to consecrate its life daily unto the Lord (see at Lev 1 and 2). In order that the whole of the daily life might be included, it was to be offered continually every morning and evening for all future time (“throughout your generations” as at <reference osisRef="Exod.12.14">Exo 12:14</reference>) at the door of the tabernacle, i.e., upon the altar erected there, before Jehovah, who would meet with the people and commune with them there (see <reference osisRef="Exod.25.22">Exo 25:22</reference>). This promise is carried out still further in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.43">Exo 29:43</reference>-46. First of all, for the purpose of elucidating and strengthening the words, “I will meet with you there” (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.42">Exo 29:42</reference>), the presence and communion of God, which are attached to the ark of the covenant in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.22">Exo 25:22</reference>, are ensured to the whole nation in the words, “And there I will meet with the children of Israel, and it (Israel) shall be sanctified through My glory.” As the people were not allowed to approach the ark of the covenant, but only to draw near to the altar of burnt-offering in the sanctuary, it was important to declare that the Lord would manifest Himself to them even there, and sanctify them by His glory. Most of the commentators have taken the altar to be the subject of “shall be sanctified;” but this is certainly an error, not only because the altar is not mentioned in the previous clause, and only slightly hinted at in the להּ in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.41">Exo 29:41</reference>, but principally because the sanctification of the altar is noticed by itself afterwards in Exo 29:44. The correct exegesis is that adopted by Baumgarten and others, who supply the word <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> (viz., regarded as a nation), which they take from the expression “children of Israel” in the previous clause. In <reference osisRef="Exod.29.44">Exo 29:44</reference>, the sanctification of the tabernacle and altar on the part of God is promised, also that of His servants, and finally, in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.45">Exo 29:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.46">Exo 29:46</reference>, the abode of God in the midst of the children of Israel, with an allusion to the blessings that would follow from Jehovah’s dwelling in the midst of them as their God (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Gen 17:7</reference>). Birth and Education of Moses. - Whilst Pharaoh was urging forward the extermination of the Israelites, God was preparing their emancipation. According to the divine purpose, the murderous edict of the king was to lead to the training and preparation of the human deliverer of Israel.  <chapter eID="Exod.29"/> <div eID="gen1056" type="x-p"/>

entries.7b9b6e577e0d908d80ddee11ce1698a393a4021a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.29.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Exod.29.1" sID="gen11718" type="section"/> <div sID="gen11719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">And this is the thing that thou shalt do unto them.</hi> Since I shall again repeat and more fully explain these things as they are written in <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.9">Leviticus 9</reference>, in the history of the consecration of the tabernacle, it will be sufficient to give nothing more than a brief summary of them here; nor is it my custom to invent mysteries out of vague speculations, <note n="174"> <div sID="gen11720" type="x-p"/> Probably the <hi type="italic">Fr., “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr">de speculations volantes</foreign>,” suggests the right reading of the <hi type="italic">Lat. </hi>here, viz., <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">alatis</hi></foreign> for <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">aliis</hi></foreign><div eID="gen11720" type="x-p"/> </note> such as may rather gratify than instruct my readers. First, since the whole human race is corrupt and infected with many impurities, so that his uncleanness prevents every single individual from having access to God, Moses, before he consecrates the priests, washes them by the sprinkling of water, in order that they may be no longer deemed to be of ordinary rank. Hence we gather that true purity and innocence, which was but typical in the Law, is found in Christ alone. “For such an high priest became us,” says the Apostle, “who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners,” to present Himself before God for us. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.7.26">Hebrews 7:26</reference>.) After they had been washed, God commands that they should be invested with the sacerdotal dress, according to their respective ranks: that the high priest should wear the ephod with the <hi type="italic">Urim </hi>and <hi type="italic">Thummim, </hi>and the mitre with the golden plate, on which shone forth “holiness to Jehovah;” and in the third place, He adds the anointing. This preparation was for the purpose of initiating them, before they performed the office of sacrificing; but it must be observed that, as to this first sacrifice, the duties which were afterwards transferred to Aaron were imposed upon Moses, as if he were the only priest; and, in point of fact, the temporal dignity which he afterwards resigned to his brother, was still in his own hands. What Moses introduces about the division of the victim, we shall more conveniently explain elsewhere, in treating of the offerings, which we have stated to be the third part of the legal worship.<div eID="gen11719" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.29.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen11718" osisID="Exod.29.1" type="section"/>
entries.6016aed4430bb31399a1b2ca664b1fbc9d440b12:
16. And thou shalt slay the ram.
